title: MAGE-RAG: Multigranular Adaptive Graph Evidence for Agentic Multimodal RAG in Long-Document QA
research_question: Can long-document multimodal question answering improve evidence coverage and control irrelevant context by dynamically constructing a query-specific page-and-element evidence subgraph under explicit budgets instead of relying on fixed top-k retrieval?
methodology: MAGE-RAG first converts each static document into a heterogeneous evidence graph containing page nodes and fine-grained element nodes such as paragraphs, tables, figures, charts, formulas, and code, connected by containment, reading-order, layout, section, and semantic-neighbor relations. At query time, an agentic controller retrieves initial pages and iteratively opens, searches, expands, and prunes graph evidence under resource budgets. A structured renderer then supplies selected page images, local element images or crops, text, and node references to a multimodal reader. The framework is evaluated on LongDocURL and MMLongBench-Doc, with ablations of page retrieval, node rendering, graph expansion, and controller behavior.

key_findings.finding: MAGE-RAG reports 52.75 overall accuracy on LongDocURL and 53.26 accuracy with 51.19 F1 on MMLongBench-Doc, showing that dynamically assembled graph evidence can be competitive with strong long-document multimodal QA baselines.
The framework shows particularly large gains on cross-page questions in MMLongBench-Doc, where its reported cross-page score is 34.70 compared with 24.87 for M3DocRAG and 24.51 for EVisRAG.

Ablations show that fine-grained node rendering and graph-neighbor expansion improve performance over page-only retrieval; graph-neighbor expansion raises the reported MMLongBench-Doc accuracy/F1 to 53.88/50.20 from 48.75/45.71 for the top-k page-only configuration.

The evidence representation preserves within-document provenance through page identifiers, element nodes, bounding boxes, image references, and page-node alignment, allowing the final reader input and controller trajectory to be inspected at multiple granularities.

The paper explicitly identifies offline parsing and evidence-graph quality as an upper bound on the system and notes that the controller adds evaluator calls and state-management cost, making the approach less compelling for short or simple single-hop documents.

limitations: The method operates on a single static document representation and does not define persistent element or region identities across successive revisions of the same attachment.
Page, node, bounding-box, and image references are useful within one parsed document but are not revision-stable lineage identifiers.
The quality ceiling depends on the offline parser, element segmentation, captions, OCR, and graph construction.
The online controller requires additional model calls and state management compared with fixed retrieval.
The authors note that the approach may not be cost-effective for short or simple single-hop documents.
Performance gains are not uniform across every benchmark slice or comparison, so the reported aggregate gains should not be interpreted as universal superiority.
raw_claims: MAGE-RAG represents long multimodal documents as graphs containing both page-level and element-level evidence.
Element nodes can carry textual content, structured content, bounding boxes, semantic types, and optional image references.
Edges encode structural and semantic relationships including containment, reading order, layout adjacency, section hierarchy, and semantic neighborhood.
The query-time controller can open, search, expand, and prune evidence rather than consuming a fixed retrieval set.
The renderer aligns selected textual evidence and visual crops with page and node references before answer generation.
Graph-neighbor expansion improves the reported QA results relative to page-only retrieval in the ablation study.
The controller trajectory records actions and retained evidence, providing an auditable retrieval trace.
The framework's performance depends on the quality of the document parser and the evidence graph constructed before querying.
The paper does not introduce a mechanism for matching the same visual region or logical element across revised versions of a document.
